newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban confront Dostum, Masood in Afghan struggle.
newsitem.headline: Taleban confront Dostum, Masood in Afghan struggle.

text.p: Islamic Taleban fighters bottled up former government forces in the Panjsher valley and confronted independent militia chief General Abdul Rashid Dostum north of Kabul on Tuesday as part of their drive to exert control over all of Afghanistan.

Taleban forces came into direct confrontation with Dostum's organised army for the first time on Monday after capturing Jabal os-Siraj, a stonghold of former government military chief Ahmed Shah Masood, 70 km (45 miles) north of Kabul, and pushing on towards the Salang Tunnel.

Dostum responded to the Taleban advance by moving tanks and artillery several km (miles) south of the strategic tunnel that links Kabul with north and central Asia, blocking further progress by the Islamic militants.

A Taleban commander at the Salang front, Mullah Ghulam Mohammad, told a visiting United Nations official in the presence of reporters that he had asked Dostum's forces to stand aside because the former communist general "does not represent the people of the north", but said Dostum appeared bent on confrontation.
Stephen Evans, a political adviser to UN special envoy to Afghanistan Norbert Holl, urged the Taleban commander to "go to Dostum's people in friendship, not in war" to try to avert further fighting.
Witnesses said scores of villagers were leaving the area in trucks piled high with belongings and heading north.

Other Taleban forces turned east from Jabal os-Siraj, capturing the town of Golbahar, 10 km (six miles) away at the foot of the Panjsher valley, homeland of Masood's mainly ethnic Tajik forces and scene of his guerrilla exploits against Soviet occupation forces in the 1980s.

Military experts said it would be hard for the Taleban to seize the rugged Panjsher unless Masood's fighters proved to have been completely demoralised by last week's loss of Kabul to the Islamic radicals.

The Taleban have given mixed signals on whether they will do battle with Dostum's well-entrenched forces. Some of their commanders say they will mop up resistance from Masood and then negotiate with Dostum.
Others say it is vital to defeat Dostum to gain control of all of Afghanistan.
"We already control most of the country but no one has recognised us yet so we have to capture all of it," one Taleban commander told reporters in Kabul.
The Taleban named a six-man interim "shura" or council led by Mullah Mohammad Rabbani, following their seizure of Kabul on Friday after Masood's forces abandoned the city.
A separate commission to govern the capital has since been set up under Mullah Turabi, who is from the southern city of Kandahar.
Taleban-controlled Kabul Radio announced several new appointments including central bank officials on Monday night.

Decisions on many issues, including the sensitive question of whether women will be allowed to work, and whether girls will be allowed to go to school, have been referred to the Taleban Kandahar-based supreme council led by Mullah Mohammad Omar, who founded the movement in 1994.

Pakistan, which has denied accusations by the former government led by President Burhanuddin Rabbani that it supports the Taleban, sent a diplomat to Kabul this week to reopen the Pakistani embassy here.

The United States has said it may send representatives to establish contact with the new rulers of the Afghan capital, but have also condemned the Taleban's summary execution of former communist president Najibullah.

On Monday, a U.S. State Department spokesman also pointed to "issues of great concern to the United States: terrorism, narcotics, human rights including due process, and the treatment of women", saying the Taleban did not control all of the country and it was not yet clear if it had set up a proper government.
"The situation on the ground is quite murky," spokesman Nicholas Burns said. He also said there was no thought being given to upgrading diplomatic ties with Afghanistan.
The United States has not had an embassy in Kabul since 1989 due to civil war and there has not been a U.S. ambassador in the country since 1979.
